definition_state.label: loneliness
definition_state.definition: A subjective negative experience characterized by dissatisfaction with the amount and/or quality of time one spends with others — experienced as a perceived mismatch between actual and desired social contact (i.e., an unmet need to belong). Loneliness can manifest as both fluctuating state feelings and more stable, trait-like experiences, is measurable with validated psychometric instruments (e.g., the Revised UCLA Loneliness Scale), and is distinct from voluntary, positively experienced solitude. Although loneliness and solitude are often conflated in the literature, solitude (operationalized in some research as the psychological experience of being alone without communication, activities, or external stimuli) is a separate construct that can co-occur with but is not equivalent to loneliness.
core_attributes: Subjective negative feeling tied to perceived social isolation
Dissatisfaction with the amount and/or quality of time spent with others (mismatch between actual and ideal)
Can manifest as both state (fluctuating) and trait (persistent) forms
Measurable with psychometric instruments (e.g., Revised UCLA Loneliness Scale)
Related to individual differences in need to belong and other self/other determinants
Distinct from voluntary preference for solitude or positively experienced alone time
Often conflated with solitude in empirical work, though solitude is the experience of being alone (without communication or activities) and may affect affective states independently
inclusion_criteria: Self-reports of distress or dissatisfaction specifically about the amount and/or quality of social contact (perceived mismatch between actual and desired social interactions)
Elevated scores on validated loneliness measures (e.g., Revised UCLA Loneliness Scale)
Evidence of either recurrent state episodes or stable, trait-like loneliness over time
Reports of subjective social disconnection rather than mere physical aloneness
exclusion_criteria: Objective social isolation without accompanying subjective distress
Voluntary preference for solitude experienced as renewal or positive aloneness (aloneliness is the opposite construct)
Being alone (solitude) per se — especially when defined as being without communication, activities, or external stimuli — when not accompanied by perceived lack of desired social contact
Temporary solitude not accompanied by perceived lack of desired social contact
definition_state.change_summary: Added nuance that loneliness is often conflated with solitude in the literature but is distinct: solitude has been operationalized as the experience of being alone without communication, activities, or stimuli and can influence affect (e.g., reduced positive affect) independently of loneliness. Clarified exclusion criteria to explicitly rule out mere physical aloneness/solitude without subjective distress.

history.change_summary: Added a literature-grounded definition emphasizing loneliness as a subjective perception of social isolation measurable by the Revised UCLA Loneliness Scale; included core attributes (persistence, social-skill links, self/other determinants) and a key exclusion distinguishing loneliness from time alone or positive solitude (Larson et al.).
history.definition: A subjective negative experience arising from perceiving oneself as socially isolated or lacking desired social connections; a measurable psychological state (e.g., via the Revised UCLA Loneliness Scale) that can persist over time and is related to individual differences (self and other determinants) and social-skill deficits. It is distinct from mere time spent alone or preference for solitude, which can be experienced as renewal rather than loneliness.

history.path: abi_phases/phases/workflows/PapersIngestionWorkflow/../../papers/paid/Coplan et al - Seeking more solitude - Conceptualization assessment and implications of aloneliness.pdf
history.change_summary: Added literature-based emphasis that loneliness reflects dissatisfaction with the amount and/or quality of time with others — a perceived mismatch between actual and ideal social contact (Perlman & Peplau; Asher & Paquette). Clarified that loneliness can be both state-like and trait-like, situated as arising from an unmet need to belong, and noted the parallel concept of aloneliness (dissatisfaction with time alone), reinforcing the distinction between loneliness and positively motivated solitude.
